children: At the 9th BW Sustainable World Conclave, sustainability and technology leaders discussed how AI is reshaping business practices while stressing the need for credible data, human oversight and responsible governance

Artificial intelligence is emerging as a tool for businesses to improve sustainability, but industry leaders at the 9th BW Sustainable World Conclave stressed that technology alone cannot solve sustainability challenges. They highlighted the importance of credible data, human judgement and organisational accountability as companies deploy AI across operations.

The panel discussion on AI and Sustainability brought together senior leaders from Reliance Industries, TÜV SÜD, Axis Bank, Cipla and Infosys to discuss how businesses are using AI and the challenges around its adoption.

Deepika Bajpai, BGM Sustainability, Reliance Industries, said businesses may have different AI use cases, but the objective is to extract greater value from data and translate it into actionable opportunities.
“The ultimate goal is very similar. and then creating new opportunities, new use cases for it moving forward,” Bajpai said.

She pointed to supply-chain sustainability and BRSR reporting as areas where AI can reduce the time spent on data collection and compliance. AI can pre-fill quantitative information, allowing teams to focus more on discussions and collaboration with value-chain partners.

Khushboo Oswal, Global Head of Carbon Management, TÜV SÜD, said certification and verification processes could also benefit from AI, particularly for repetitive tasks such as reviewing evidence and processing information.

“AI definitely helps to process and try to make the process efficient,” Oswal said. However, she stressed that AI-generated outputs still require human validation. “Not that we trust what entirely comes out of AI,” she added.
Data Quality Remains Critical
Abhijit Agarwal, Head Sustainability and CSR, Axis Bank, said AI should be treated as a means of improving existing processes rather than an objective in itself.
“Ultimately, my understanding is AI is not an end in itself. Ultimately, it is serving a purpose,” Agarwal said.

He cited applications in banking including data validation, risk management, customer onboarding and operations, while noting that Axis Bank has introduced Axiom, an enterprise-level AI model with applications across the bank.

For the pharmaceutical sector, the stakes around AI-generated information can be particularly high. Rajesh Vasudevan, Chief Corporate EHS and Sustainability, Cipla, said the industry relies on maker-checker processes because of their implications for patient and employee safety.
“The part which AI can play is more on a maker, but the checker part still has to be a human interface,” Vasudevan said, pointing to the risk of hallucinations and inconsistent AI outputs.

Swapnil Joshi, Director in Industrial Principles, Sustainability and Climate Tech, Smart Infrastructure, Head APAC in India, Infosys, similarly argued that AI should be viewed as an enabler rather than a standalone solution.
“I would gently push back on aspects, or on the theme which says that AI solves sustainability problems. It does not. I think AI enables solving sustainability problems,” Joshi said.

He distinguished between “efficiency AI”, which can optimise processes and predict outcomes, and “strategy AI”, which can contribute to product and business development. However, he cautioned that incomplete or fragmented data can produce misleading results.
“When you start feeding the models with incomplete, fragmented, or disproportionate data, what comes out is a very confident but incorrect output,” Joshi said.
Accountability Stays With Organisations

The panel also discussed AI's role in addressing social sustainability issues. Joshi cited an Infosys programme with a large healthcare client in the UK that uses AI to identify modern slavery risks across supply chains.

Bajpai said technology can amplify sustainability challenges while also helping organisations identify emerging risks when deployed responsibly. “Technology is only as good as the person using it,” she said, highlighting the need for ethics and regulatory considerations.

Vasudevan said the responsibility for AI-generated outcomes ultimately cannot be delegated to the technology itself. “Ultimately, the governance or the accountability still lies with the organisation,” he said.

The discussion concluded that AI can improve sustainability processes, support risk identification and make data-intensive activities more efficient, but its effectiveness depends on data quality, governance and human oversight.
Sonali Chawhan
